title: Conditional Flow Models for Offline Maximum Entropy Reinforcement Learning

paper.title: Conditional Flow Models for Offline Maximum Entropy Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract:
Abstract Offline maximum entropy reinforcement learning seeks to estimate the optimal soft action-value function Q ∗ Q^{*} from a fixed dataset without further interaction with the environment. Although Q ∗ Q^{*} is characterized by the soft optimal Bellman equation, the corresponding Bellman operator cannot be evaluated directly because both the reward distribution and the transition kernel are unknown. Consequently, estimating Q ∗ Q^{*} requires the joint treatment of environment modeling and value function learning.
We propose a framework that addresses these tasks separately. Conditional diffusion models based on probability flow ODEs estimate the conditional reward distribution and transition kernel. The resulting distributional estimators define a data driven approximation of the soft optimal Bellman operator, whose empirical Bellman residual is minimized over a class of deep neural networks to estimate Q ∗ Q^{*} . This formulation separates high dimensional conditional distribution estimation from Bellman fixed point estimation while preserving the structure of the maximum entropy Bellman equation.
We establish nonasymptotic guarantees for the proposed method. For operator learning, we derive total variation error bounds for the conditional flow estimators that account explicitly for score estimation, numerical discretization, and terminal smoothing. For soft value learning, we first use the soft Bellman equation to show that Q ∗ Q^{*} inherits Hölder regularity from the conditional reward and transition densities. For any Hölder index β \beta ,
the value learning stage achieves an excess Bellman residual risk bound of order 𝒪 ~ ​ ( n − 2 ​ β d + 2 ​ β ) , \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(n^{-\frac{2\beta}{d+2\beta}}\big), where d d is the total dimension of the state and action spaces.
In contrast to many existing theoretical analyses of deep reinforcement learning, our results do not require Bellman completeness. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. KEY WORDS :
Deep maximum entropy RL,
Bellman residual minimization,
Deep Q ∗ Q^{\ast} estimation, Conditional flow model.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reinforcement learning (RL) studies sequential decision making in Markov decision processes, where an agent learns from observations, actions, and rewards to improve long-term performance ( Kaelbling et al., 1996 ; Sutton and Barto, 2018 ) . Classical methods represent value functions or policies explicitly, whereas deep reinforcement learning uses neural networks to handle large or continuous state and action spaces. This combination has enabled progress in visual control and game playing ( Mnih et al., 2015 ; Silver et al., 2016 ) , as well as applications to chip placement and plasma control ( Mirhoseini et al., 2021 ; Degrave et al., 2022 ) . These applications illustrate the flexibility of neural representations, while also making the statistical behavior of value estimation an important theoretical question. In value-based methods, the fitted target contains a continuation value estimated from data. Consequently, errors in Bellman-target construction interact with neural network approximation and empirical optimization. Actor-critic methods introduce a further interaction because policy updates depend on an estimated critic, while the critic is trained using data and targets associated with the policy ( Fujimoto et al., 2018 ; Haarnoja et al., 2018b ) . In the offline setting, the available dataset is fixed and additional environment interaction is unavailable. A useful analysis must explain how offline data are used to estimate the Bellman operator and how operator estimation error propagates to the learned value function. Maximum entropy RL augments the expected-return objective with policy entropy, encouraging stochastic policies while retaining a preference for actions with high expected return ( Ziebart et al., 2008 ; Haarnoja et al., 2018b ; Levine, 2018 ) . Entropy regularization replaces action maximization in the optimal Bellman equation with a log-partition operation. The resulting operator is associated with a Gibbs policy whose density depends on the soft action-value function ( Geist et al., 2019 ) . This structure connects value function estimation with policy optimization: the soft value summarizes an integral over actions, and the estimated action-value function determines the corresponding policy. Soft Q-learning develops this connection through energy-based policies and approximate inference ( Haarnoja et al., 2017 ; Levine, 2018 ) . Path Consistency Learning uses temporal consistency relations involving values and entropy-regularized action probabilities ( Nachum et al., 2017 ) , while Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) combines a stochastic actor, a soft critic, and replay data for continuous control ( Haarnoja et al., 2018b ; Haarnoja et al., 2018c ) . The relationship between policy gradients and soft Q-learning provides a complementary account of their shared optimality structure ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) . Soft policy-gradient methods and robust-control analyses further develop the algorithmic and theoretical consequences of entropy regularization ( Shi et al., 2019 ; Eysenbach and Levine, 2022 ) . For offline estimation, however, the soft Bellman operator still involves a conditional expectation over the unknown next-state distribution. Evaluating this expectation, together with the action integral, is the statistical and computational problem addressed by the present construction. Model-based RL provides a natural way to address this difficulty by explicitly learning the reward or transition dynamics from data and then using the learned model for planning, synthetic data generation, or Bellman evaluation ( Sutton and Barto, 2018 ; Janner et al., 2019 ; Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) . This paradigm is particularly attractive when real environment interaction is expensive or unavailable, since the learned dynamics can be queried repeatedly. Its central challenge is model bias: inaccuracies in the learned dynamics may accumulate over long imagined rollouts and can be amplified by subsequent policy optimization. Existing approaches such as MBPO, MOPO, and MOReL mitigate this effect through short model rollouts or conservative and uncertainty-aware objectives ( Janner et al., 2019 ; Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) . This perspective suggests learning the conditional next state law directly and using it locally to approximate the conditional expectation appearing in the soft Bellman operator. Recent advances in generative flow models have provided flexible tools for representing complex distributions in reinforcement learning. Existing flow based reinforcement learning methods mainly use flows on the decision side to model behavior policies, represent multimodal action distributions, or generate high value actions. For example, Flow Q Learning uses a flow matching policy to capture complex behavior distributions and introduces an auxiliary one step policy to avoid backpropagation through the full iterative sampling procedure ( Park et al., 2025 ) . Energy guided and value guided flow methods further combine generative flow sampling with value functions or energy signals to improve action generation and policy optimization ( Alles et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Feng et al., 2025 ) . These studies demonstrate the strong distributional modeling capability of flow models in reinforcement learning. However, this capability can also be used on the environment side. In particular, a conditional flow model can approximate the full transition law P ⁡ ( S ′ | s , a ) P(S^{\prime}|s,a) rather than only predicting the conditional mean of the next state. Repeated samples generated from the learned transition law can then be used to approximate the conditional expectation appearing in the soft Bellman operator. Motivated by these developments, we propose a framework for offline maximum entropy value learning that integrates conditional probability flow modeling with soft Bellman residual risk. Conditional probability flow ODEs estimate the conditional reward law and transition law from batch data. The learned reward and transition distributions are incorporated into the soft optimal Bellman operator. With the learned environment model held fixed, the optimal soft action value function Q ∗ Q^{*} is estimated by minimizing the empirical soft Bellman residual over a ReLU DNN class. Unlike existing flow based reinforcement learning methods that mainly use flow models to represent policies or generate actions, our flow models operate on the environment side and model both the reward and the next state conditional on ( s , a ) (s,a) . This construction separates environment law estimation from soft Bellman residual risk, enables repeated sampling from the learned reward and transition distributions, and avoids jointly optimizing the environment model and the value function within a single coupled objective. We derive a nonasymptotic bound on the squared Bellman-residual risk. The bound separates the error in the learned operator from the statistical and approximation terms associated with residual minimization. Under the stated conditions, the latter terms are of order O ~ ( n − 2 β / ( d + 2 β ) ) \widetilde{O}(n^{-2\beta/(d+2\beta)}) , where n n is the value learning sample size, d d is the state-action dimension, and β \beta is the Hölder smoothness of Q ∗ Q^{*} . Importantly, our analysis does not require the Bellman completeness assumption commonly adopted in theoretical studies of deep reinforcement learning ( Uehara et al., 2023 ; Zhan et al., 2022 ) . Empirically, we evaluate the proposed method in three experimental settings: a simulated MDP, classical control tasks, and HalfCheetah datasets from D4RL ( Fu et al., 2020 ) . We compare the proposed method with SAC ( Haarnoja et al., 2018a ) , CQL ( Kumar et al., 2020 ) , and MOPO ( Yu et al., 2020 ) . The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of using conditional probability flow models to estimate the reward and transition laws and support the separation of environment law estimation from soft value function learning.

sections.heading: 1.1 Contributions
sections.text: The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows. • We develop a framework for offline maximum entropy RL that separates conditional environment modeling from soft value learning. Conditional probability flow ODEs learn the reward distribution and transition kernel, and samples generated from these models define a data-driven approximation of the soft optimal Bellman operator. We then estimate Q ∗ Q^{\ast} by minimizing the empirical soft Bellman residual over a class of ReLU DNNs. This formulation allows the environment modeling and value learning errors to be analyzed separately. Numerical results show that the proposed method achieves competitive performance across the considered offline control tasks. • We decompose the error of the proposed estimator into operator estimation and value learning terms. The operator error is controlled by total variation bounds for the learned reward and transition laws. We further establish that the Hölder regularity of the conditional densities with respect to the state-action variables is inherited by Q ∗ Q^{*} through the soft Bellman equation. This result yields rates for the value learning stage without a separate smoothness assumption on Q ∗ Q^{*} or a Bellman completeness condition. Combining these results, we obtain nonasymptotic bounds on the operator estimation error and the Bellman residual risk of the resulting action-value estimator.

sections.heading: Deep RL and Max Entropy RL.
sections.text: DRL combines sequential decision making with neural function approximation, allowing value functions and policies to be learned from high dimensional observations ( Sutton and Barto, 2018 ; Mnih et al., 2015 ) . Its main difficulty is that the learning target is endogenous: a value estimate is reused to construct later temporal difference targets, while a policy update changes the distribution from which future data are collected ( Sutton and Barto, 2018 ; Jiao et al., 2025 ) . DRL algorithms therefore differ largely in how they control errors, distribution shift, and the interaction between policy evaluation and policy improvement ( Sutton and Barto, 2018 ; Mnih et al., 2015 ; Jiao et al., 2025 ) . In discrete action spaces, DQN established a practical value-based template by combining a convolutional Q-network with experience replay and a slowly updated target network ( Mnih et al., 2015 ) . Replay improves data reuse and weakens short range temporal dependence, whereas the target network slows the change of the Bellman target ( Mnih et al., 2015 ) . Double DQN reduces maximization bias by separating action selection from action evaluation ( van Hasselt et al., 2016 ) ; the dueling architecture decomposes the output into state value and advantage streams ( Wang et al., 2016 ) ; and distributional RL models the return distribution rather than only its expectation ( Bellemare et al., 2017 ) . These refinements improve target construction or representation, but the learned Q-function is still defined through a recursive Bellman relation and remains sensitive to approximation error in weakly sampled regions ( Sutton and Barto, 2018 ; Fujimoto et al., 2018 ; Jiao et al., 2025 ) . Maximum entropy RL modifies this conventional objective by maximizing expected return together with the policy entropy. The resulting soft Bellman backup replaces action maximization by a log-sum-exp (or log partition) operation, and its optimal policy is the corresponding Gibbs distribution ( Ziebart et al., 2008 ; Levine, 2018 ; Geist et al., 2019 ) . This formulation preserves multiple competitive actions, which can improve exploration and robustness when the value landscape is multimodal. In deep continuous-control settings, soft Q-learning introduced energy-based stochastic policies ( Haarnoja et al., 2017 ) , while SAC made the maximum entropy objective practical through off policy replay, separate actor and critic networks, and an adaptive temperature variant ( Haarnoja et al., 2018b ; Haarnoja et al., 2018c ) . Path Consistency Learning offers a complementary view by enforcing multi-step soft consistency between values and entropy regularized policy probabilities ( Nachum et al., 2017 ) . These methods differ in parameterization and optimization, but all use entropy regularization to couple policy improvement with soft value estimation. Further studies have expanded both the algorithmic and theoretical foundations of learning with entropy regularization. The equivalence between policy gradient methods and soft Q-learning reveals that maximum entropy methods based on value functions and those based on policies share the same underlying optimization structure ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) . Deep Soft Policy Gradient provides an alternative implementation of the maximum entropy objective in continuous action spaces by combining actor and critic networks with off-policy learning ( Shi et al., 2019 ) . For offline learning, minimax soft-Q learning provides guarantees under realizability and partial coverage ( Uehara et al., 2023 ) ; separately, robust control results show that MaxEnt RL can solve classes of RL problems with reward and transition uncertainty ( Eysenbach and Levine, 2022 ) . Together, these studies connect entropy regularization to algorithm design and statistical guarantees, while leaving open the question of how transition model error affects soft Bellman value learning. Continuous control makes explicit maximization over actions impractical and motivates policy gradient and actor–critic methods ( Konda and Tsitsiklis, 1999 ; Silver et al., 2014 ) . In an actor–critic architecture, the actor represents the policy, while the critic estimates a value or advantage used to reduce gradient variance ( Konda and Tsitsiklis, 1999 ; Mnih et al., 2016 ) . This two line organization is flexible, but it creates coupled optimization: the critic is fitted using data from a changing actor, and the actor is updated using a critic that is only approximately accurate ( Konda and Tsitsiklis, 1999 ; Fujimoto et al., 2018 ) . Deterministic policy gradient methods differentiate the critic with respect to the action and backpropagate this derivative through the actor ( Silver et al., 2014 ) . DDPG combines this mechanism with replay and target networks to obtain an off policy algorithm for continuous actions ( Lillicrap et al., 2016 ) . Its deterministic actor is efficient, but exploration must be injected separately and the actor may exploit local overestimation in the critic ( Lillicrap et al., 2016 ; Fujimoto et al., 2018 ) . TD3 addresses this failure mode through clipped double-Q targets, delayed actor updates, and target policy smoothing ( Fujimoto et al., 2018 ) . These changes improve robustness without removing the fundamental dependence of policy improvement on an estimated critic ( Fujimoto et al., 2018 ) . Explicit environment modeling is central to our setting. Direct DRL methods construct Bellman targets from observed transitions without first estimating a separate transition kernel, whereas model-based methods estimate rewards or dynamics and use the learned model for planning, synthetic data generation, or Bellman evaluation ( Sutton and Barto, 2018 ; Janner et al., 2019 ; Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) . Explicit modeling can improve data reuse, but inaccurate models may be exploited by the policy and multi-step rollouts can accumulate error ( Janner et al., 2019 ; Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) . MBPO limits this effect with short rollouts initialized from real data ( Janner et al., 2019 ) ; MOPO and MOReL introduce pessimism or uncertainty control in offline model-based learning ( Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) . Our framework learns the conditional next state law, but uses it only for the one step expectation in the soft Bellman operator rather than for long imagined trajectories. This localized construction makes transition error visible at the operator level and separates it from the statistical and approximation errors of Bellman residual value estimation, in contrast to the repeated model rollout used in MBPO, MOPO, and MOReL ( Janner et al., 2019 ; Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) .

sections.heading: Flow-based RL.
sections.text: Generative modeling has broadened the policy and trajectory distributions available to RL algorithms ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2025 ) . A conventional continuous control actor is often a deterministic map or a diagonal Gaussian distribution ( Lillicrap et al., 2016 ; Haarnoja et al., 2018b ) . Although computationally convenient, such a representation can be inadequate when a state admits several qualitatively different yet individually valid actions; a unimodal actor may average incompatible modes and place mass on actions that are poorly supported by the data ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2023 ; Celik et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2025 ) . Diffusion and flow matching models instead transport a simple reference distribution into a complex conditional distribution, making multimodal action sequences, policies, or trajectories directly representable ( Song et al., 2021 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ; Albergo et al., 2025 ) . This flexibility is particularly attractive in offline RL, goal conditioned control, imitation learning, and robotic manipulation, where datasets may contain several successful behavioral strategies ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2025 ) . For flow-based generative policies in particular, direct policy improvement through an iterative flow remains difficult because the terminal action depends on every integration step ( Park et al., 2025 ; Alles et al., 2025 ) . Flow Q-Learning (FQL) separates distribution modeling from Q-based improvement ( Park et al., 2025 ) . It first fits a flow matching policy to a potentially multimodal behavior distribution, then trains an auxiliary one-step policy with a Q-learning objective and links the two through a distillation style loss ( Park et al., 2025 ) . The construction avoids backpropagating the RL objective through the complete flow trajectory and removes iterative sampling at test time ( Park et al., 2025 ) . The flow supplies an expressive behavioral prior, whereas the one-step policy provides a tractable object for value improvement ( Park et al., 2025 ) . Importantly, the flow in FQL models the conditional action distribution and is therefore a policy generator, not an estimator of the environment transition law ( Park et al., 2025 ) . A second group of methods incorporates energy or value information directly into the probability path. FlowQ absorbs energy guidance into the learned velocity field rather than repeatedly applying an external guidance term during inference ( Alles et al., 2025 ) . Energy weighted flow matching reweights the flow objective so that the terminal distribution approximates an energy tilted reference distribution, with a learned Q-function providing the energy in offline RL ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . General analyses of flow guidance describe how conditional expectations, energy gradients, and approximations of intermediate guided marginals determine the corrected velocity field ( Feng et al., 2025 ) . Diffusion guidance can likewise be interpreted as a controllable policy improvement operator, where the guidance scale balances fidelity to a reference generator against movement toward critic preferred actions ( Frans et al., 2025 ) . Maximum entropy approaches such as DIME and MaxEntDP use expressive diffusion policies to retain multiple high value action modes rather than collapsing to a single deterministic decision ( Celik et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2025 ) . These methods primarily improve the representation of the policy π ⁡ ( a | s ) \pi(a|s) ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2025 ; Alles et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Celik et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2025 ) . They do not, by themselves, identify the environmental transition law P ⁡ ( s ′ | s , a ) P(s^{\prime}|s,a) , because the generators in these methods are trained as action or trajectory models rather than conditional next state models ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2025 ; Alles et al., 2025 ) . This distinction is essential for maximum entropy value learning because the soft Bellman target contains both an action side log partition operation and an expectation over the next state distribution ( Haarnoja et al., 2018b ; Geist et al., 2019 ) . An action flow can generate diverse actions, but without environment interaction or a separate dynamics model it cannot generate corresponding next states ( Park et al., 2025 ; Alles et al., 2025 ) ; conversely, a learned transition model can sample next states conditional on ( s , a ) (s,a) but does not automatically define an improved policy ( Janner et al., 2019 ; Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) . Policy flow methods therefore address multimodal action representation and value guidance, whereas our method addresses conditional transition estimation and the effect of transition error on the soft Bellman operator ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2025 ; Alles et al., 2025 ; Janner et al., 2019 ; Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) . In contrast, our method uses flows to learn the reward and transition distributions, which are then used to construct an empirical Bellman operator for value function learning.

3 Flow-Based Soft Value Learning
sections.text: In this section, we propose our framework for estimating the optimal soft action-value function Q ∗ Q^{*} from offline data by integrating conditional environment distribution learning with empirical Bellman residual minimization. Conditional probability flow ODEs transport Gaussian noise to the conditional reward law ℛ ( ⋅ | s , a ) \mathcal{R}(\cdot|s,a) and transition kernel 𝒫 ( ⋅ | s , a ) \mathcal{P}(\cdot|s,a) . Their velocity fields are estimated by denoising score matching and simulated through EM discretization, yielding the conditional samplers ℛ ^ ( ⋅ | s , a ) \widehat{\mathcal{R}}(\cdot|s,a) and 𝒫 ^ ( ⋅ | s , a ) \widehat{\mathcal{P}}(\cdot|s,a) from the offline datasets 𝔻 r \mathbb{D}_{r} and 𝔻 x \mathbb{D}_{x} (see section 2.2 ). Samples generated from these learned laws approximate the reward and next state expectations, while importance sampling approximates the log-partition continuation value. These components define a data driven soft optimal Bellman operator 𝒯 ^ α \widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{\alpha} , whose empirical Bellman residual is minimized over a bounded ReLU DNN class on the independent dataset 𝕊 \mathbb{S} to obtain Q ^ \widehat{Q} . The resulting procedure forms a complete pipeline from conditional environment distribution learning to soft value function estimation and preserves the sample separation required for the theoretical analysis. We first define the residual loss under the optimal policy, ℒ π ∗ ​ ( 𝒯 α ∗ , Q ) := 𝔼 ( S , A ) ∼ μ π ∗ ​ | 𝒯 α ∗ ​ Q ​ ( S , A ) − Q ⁡ ( S , A ) | 2 . \mathcal{L}_{\pi^{*}}(\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}^{*};Q):=\mathbb{E}_{(S,A)\sim\mu_{\pi^{*}}}\left|\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}^{*}Q(S,A)-Q(S,A)\right|^{2}. If μ π ∗ ≪ μ π b \mu_{\pi^{*}}\ll\mu_{\pi_{b}} and the density ratio d ​ μ π ∗ d ​ μ π b \frac{\mathrm{d}\mu_{\pi^{*}}}{\mathrm{d}\mu_{\pi_{b}}} has a finite second moment under μ π b \mu_{\pi_{b}} , then by Lemma D.1 , we have ( ℒ π ∗ ​ ( 𝒯 α ∗ , Q ) ) 2 ≲ Q max 2 ​ ℒ ​ ( 𝒯 α ∗ , Q ) , \bigl(\mathcal{L}_{\pi^{*}}(\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}^{*};Q)\bigr)^{2}\lesssim Q_{\max}^{2}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}^{*};Q), where ℒ ⁡ ( 𝒯 α ∗ , Q ) \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}^{*};Q) denotes the population Bellman residual loss for offline observations collected under the behavior policy π b \pi_{b} , defined by ℒ ⁡ ( 𝒯 α ∗ , Q ) := 𝔼 ( S , A ) ∼ μ ​ | 𝒯 α ∗ ​ Q ​ ( S , A ) − Q ⁡ ( S , A ) | 2 , \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}^{*};Q):=\mathbb{E}_{(S,A)\sim\mu}\left|\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}^{*}Q(S,A)-Q(S,A)\right|^{2}, (1) with μ = μ π b \mu=\mu_{\pi_{b}} . Under the Hölder continuity condition on the conditional densities specified in Assumption 4.4 , we apply Lemmas A.6 and D.1 to express our objective as the minimization of the Bellman residual loss under the behavior distribution: Q ∗ ∈ arg ⁡ min Q ⁡ ℒ ⁡ ( 𝒯 α ∗ , Q ) . Q^{*}\in\arg\min_{Q}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}^{*};Q). In offline learning, the true operator is unavailable because the conditional reward and transition laws are unknown. The learned conditional samplers above provide its data driven approximation. We present the conditional flow construction for the next-state variable X = S ′ X=S^{\prime} learned from 𝔻 x \mathbb{D}_{x} . The reward model follows the same construction with X X replaced by R R and 𝔻 x \mathbb{D}_{x} by 𝔻 r \mathbb{D}_{r} .

Remark 4.2 . Theorem 4.3 separates the excess Bellman residual risk into value learning and operator-learning errors. The value learning term Q max 2 ​ n − 2 ​ β d + 2 ​ β ​ log 3 ​ n Q_{\max}^{2}n^{- rac{2 eta}{d+2 eta}}\log^{3}n combines the statistical and ReLU approximation errors. The operator learning error consists of the conditional flow error Q max 2 ​ ( ζ τ 4 + Δ 2 τ 8 ​ log 2 ​ τ + τ β ∧ 1 ) Q_{\max}^{2} ig( rac{\zeta}{	au^{4}}+ rac{\Delta^{2}}{	au^{8}}\log^{2}	au+	au^{ eta\wedge 1} ig) , corresponding respectively to score estimation, EM discretization, and terminal smoothing, together with the Monte-Carlo error and the importance sampling error. Ignoring logarithmic factors, the resulting rate is 𝒪 ⁡ ( n − 2 ​ β d + 2 ​ β ) \mathcal{O} ig(n^{- rac{2 eta}{d+2 eta}} ig) . For context, existing entropy regularized RL theory reports rates under rather different settings. Uehara et al. (2023) study offline minimax soft Q learning and obtain a 𝒪 ~ ( n − 1 / 4 ) \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{-1/4}) statistical error for soft Q Q estimation and policy regret under realizability and partial coverage. Dai et al. (2018) propose Smoothed Bellman Error Embedding for reinforcement learning with nonlinear function approximation and obtain a statistical Bellman error term 𝒪 ( n − 1 / 2 ) \mathcal{O}(n^{-1/2}) for a single β  eta -mixing off-policy trajectory. These results are not directly comparable with our excess Bellman residual bound, but they give useful reference points for rates in entropy regularized reinforcement learning. A key feature of our theoretical analysis is that it does not require Bellman completeness. The approximation error depends only on the fixed target Q ∗ Q^{*} through inf Q ∈ 𝒬 ‖ Q − Q ∗ ‖ ∞ 2 \inf\limits_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}}\|Q-Q^{*}\|_{\infty}^{2} , rather than on the Bellman images of all functions in 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} . Consequently, the Hölder regularity of Q ∗ Q^{*} and the approximation capacity of ReLU DNNs suffice to control this error. This feature follows from estimating the soft Bellman operator before performing Bellman residual minimization and distinguishes our approach from recursive methods that repeatedly project Bellman updates onto a prescribed function class. This approach also differs from existing minimax formulations and methods based on primal and dual optimization for offline reinforcement learning with entropy regularization ( Uehara et al., 2023 ; Zhan et al., 2022 ) .

sections.heading: 5 Numerical Experiments
sections.text: In this section, we consider three groups of offline control experiments. We first study a fully specified simulated MDP with a three-component transition kernel and a two-component reward law, then consider three classical continuous-control tasks, and finally evaluate on four HalfCheetah datasets from D4RL. In every group, the proposed method is compared with offline SAC ( Haarnoja et al., 2018a ) , CQL ( Kumar et al., 2020 ) , and MOPO ( Yu et al., 2020 ) using fixed offline data. Evaluation trajectories are never added to the training datasets.

sections.heading: 5.2 Classical continuous-control tasks.
sections.text: In this section, we compare the methods on three tasks: standard Pendulum, a stochastic inverted pendulum, and a stochastic five-mode MountainCar. Ordinary Pendulum follows the deterministic Pendulum-v1 dynamics with state ( θ , θ ˙ ) (\theta,\dot{\theta}) , bounded torque, a 200-step horizon, and the standard quadratic control cost. The stochastic version adds an actuator disturbance in { − 0.45 , 0 , 0.45 } \{-0.45,0,0.45\} with probabilities ( 0.20 , 0.60 , 0.20 ) (0.20,0.60,0.20) and Gaussian acceleration noise with standard deviation 0.08 0.08 . MountainCar uses position and velocity as its state, terminates upon reaching the goal or after 999 steps, and adds one of five equally likely wind accelerations ( − 0.0008 , − 0.0004 , 0 , 0.0004 , 0.0008 ) (-0.0008,-0.0004,0,0.0004,0.0008) at every transition. For Pendulum and stochastic inverted pendulum, the behavior policy chooses a uniform random torque with probability 0.80 0.80 and a noisy upright PD action otherwise. Each retained transition follows L ∼ Unif ⁡ { 0 , … , 79 } L\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{0,\ldots,79\} behavior steps from an independent reset. sections.heading: 5.3 D4RL HalfCheetah.
sections.text: Finally, we evaluate the proposed method on HalfCheetah from the D4RL benchmark ( Fu et al., 2020 ) , using fixed offline datasets without additional data collection during optimization. HalfCheetah is a continuous control task in which a planar articulated agent applies bounded joint torques to move forward. The task is sensitive to the learned action distribution, as locally supported actions may eventually lead to states poorly represented in the offline data. We consider four datasets that differ in behavior quality and state-action coverage. Random contains transitions from a random policy, providing broad coverage but low returns, while Medium contains data from a partially trained policy with moderate performance. Medium-Replay comprises the replay buffer accumulated during training of the medium policy, combining behavior from early and later training stages. Full-Replay spans a longer period of policy improvement and provides broader replay coverage. All methods are trained for 1M gradient updates with the temperature parameter fixed at α = 0.2 \alpha=0.2 . The final results are obtained from the models after 1M updates. Each final policy is evaluated for 100 episodes, and Table 3 reports the mean and standard deviation of the resulting episode returns. The proposed method uses a conditional Gaussian proposal distribution parameterized by the current state, followed by a hyperbolic tangent transformation. A latent action z z is sampled from a diagonal Gaussian distribution, and the bounded action a a is obtained as z ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ θ ​ ( s ) , diag ⁡ ( σ θ 2 ​ ( s ) ) ) , a = tanh ⁡ ( z ) . z\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\mu_{\theta}(s),\operatorname{diag}\left(\sigma_{\theta}^{2}(s)\right)\right),~a=\tanh(z). The mean depends on the current state and determines where the proposal probability is concentrated. The scale parameter controls the dispersion of candidate actions around that region. The transformation ensures that each sampled action satisfies the bounds of the HalfCheetah action space. We report performance using the D4RL normalized score. Given an average undiscounted return R R , the normalized score is defined as Score D4RL ⁡ ( R ) = 100 × R − R random R expert − R random , \operatorname{Score}_{\mathrm{D4RL}}(R)=100\times\frac{R-R_{\mathrm{random}}}{R_{\mathrm{expert}}-R_{\mathrm{random}}}, (2) where R random R_{\mathrm{random}} and R expert R_{\mathrm{expert}} denote the random policy and expert policy reference returns provided by D4RL for HalfCheetah. This transformation assigns a score of zero to the random policy reference and a score of 100 to the expert policy reference. All methods are normalized using the same reference returns. On Medium-Replay, it obtains 48.88 ± 0.78 48.88\pm 0.78 , outperforming CQL ( 47.02 ± 0.79 47.02\pm 0.79 ) and SAC ( 33.03 ± 16.75 33.03\pm 16.75 ), while remaining below MOPO ( 50.87 ± 19.95 50.87\pm 19.95 ) with substantially lower evaluation variability. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: This work studies the estimation of the optimal soft action value function Q ∗ Q^{*} from offline data in maximum entropy reinforcement learning. We use conditional probability flow ODEs to learn the reward and transition laws and construct an approximation of the soft optimal Bellman operator. The value function is then fitted by minimizing the empirical residual of this operator. Learning the environment model before fitting the value function allows us to distinguish the errors introduced at each stage and study their effect on the final residual risk. The analysis relies on approximating Q ∗ Q^{*} itself, without imposing Bellman completeness on the neural network class. For the value learning stage, the statistical error and the ReLU approximation error together contribute 𝒪 ⁡ ( n − 2 ​ β d + 2 ​ β ) \mathcal{O}\bigl(n^{-\frac{2\beta}{d+2\beta}}\bigr) to the excess Bellman residual risk, up to logarithmic factors. The remaining error comes from approximating the soft Bellman operator. Its conditional flow component is bounded by 𝒪 ⁡ ( ζ τ 4 + Δ 2 τ 8 + τ β ∧ 1 ) \mathcal{O}\bigl(\frac{\zeta}{\tau^{4}}+\frac{\Delta^{2}}{\tau^{8}}+\tau^{\beta\wedge 1}\bigr) , with the three terms arising from score estimation, numerical discretization, and terminal smoothing. Monte-Carlo averaging over generated rewards and next states adds a contribution of 𝒪 ⁡ ( n d d + 2 ​ β m ) \mathcal{O}\bigl(\frac{n^{\frac{d}{d+2\beta}}}{m}\bigr) , while importance sampling for the soft state value introduces 𝒪 ⁡ ( n d d + 2 ​ β M ) \mathcal{O}\bigl(\frac{n^{\frac{d}{d+2\beta}}}{M}\bigr) . Logarithmic factors are omitted from these expressions. With the assumptions and parameter choices in the main theorem, the operator learning terms are controlled at the same order as the value learning term. The resulting excess Bellman residual risk therefore has the nonparametric rate 𝒪 ⁡ ( n − 2 ​ β d + 2 ​ β ) \mathcal{O}\bigl(n^{-\frac{2\beta}{d+2\beta}}\bigr) , up to logarithmic factors, without requiring Bellman completeness. The numerical experiments complement these guarantees and illustrate the effectiveness of the method on the tasks considered. Building on these results, future work could study offline policy optimization and examine how the approach scales to higher dimensional continuous control. Extending the framework to partially observed environments and larger world models would also broaden its range of applications.

sections.heading: Appendix
sections.text: The appendices follow the structure of the theoretical analysis. Appendices B and C prove the operator learning and value learning theorems, respectively. Building on these results, Appendix D characterizes the population residual objective, establishes the error decomposition lemma, and proves the main theorem. Appendix E collects the auxiliary lemmas used in these proofs.

sections.heading: Appendix A Proof Outline
sections.text: The preceding section states the soft operator learning, value learning, and overall guarantees. We now explain how the two intermediate bounds are obtained and how they combine to prove Theorem 4.3 . The argument begins with the following decomposition of the excess Bellman residual risk; its full proof is provided in Appendix D . Lemma A.1 (Error decomposition) . Conditional on 𝔻 , 𝕋 , ℤ \mathbb{D},\mathbb{T},\mathbb{Z} , the estimator Q ^ \widehat{Q} satisfies 𝔼 𝕊 ​ [ ℒ ⁡ ( 𝒯 α ∗ , Q ^ ) − ℒ ⁡ ( 𝒯 α ∗ , Q ∗ ) ] \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{S}}\left[\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}^{*};\widehat{Q})-\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}^{*};Q^{*})\right] ≤ 2 ​ 𝔼 𝕊 ​ [ ‖ 𝒯 α ∗ ​ Q ^ − 𝒯 ^ α ​ Q ^ ‖ L 2 ​ ( μ ) 2 ] ⏟ Part ​ 𝐈 + 8 ​ ‖ 𝒯 ^ α ​ Q ∗ − 𝒯 α ∗ ​ Q ∗ ‖ L 2 ​ ( μ ) 2 ⏟ Part ​ 𝐈𝐈 \displaystyle\leq\underbrace{2\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{S}}\left[\|{\cal T}^{*}_{\alpha}\widehat{Q}-\widehat{{\cal T}}_{\alpha}\widehat{Q}\|_{L^{2}(\mu)}^{2}\right]}_{\mathrm{Part}~\mathbf{I}}+\underbrace{8\|\widehat{{\cal T}}_{\alpha}Q^{*}-{\cal T}^{*}_{\alpha}Q^{*}\|_{L^{2}(\mu)}^{2}}_{\mathrm{Part}~\mathbf{II}} + 2 ​ 𝔼 𝕊 ​ sup Q ∈ 𝒬 ( ℒ ⁡ ( 𝒯 ^ α , Q ) − 2 ​ ℒ ^ ​ ( 𝒯 ^ α , Q ) ) + 8 ​ ( 1 + γ ) 2 ​ inf Q ∈ 𝒬 ‖ Q − Q ∗ ‖ ∞ 2 ⏟ Part ​ 𝐈𝐈𝐈 . \displaystyle+\underbrace{2\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{S}}\sup_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}}\Big({\cal L}(\widehat{{\cal T}}_{\alpha};Q)-2\widehat{{\cal L}}(\widehat{{\cal T}}_{\alpha};Q)\Big)+8(1+\gamma)^{2}\inf_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}}\|Q-Q^{*}\|_{\infty}^{2}}_{\mathrm{Part}~\mathbf{III}}. Parts I and II evaluate the discrepancy between the true and learned Bellman operators at Q ^ \widehat{Q} and Q ∗ Q^{*} , respectively. They quantify how errors in estimating the conditional reward law and transition kernel propagate to the Bellman operator. Part III contains the statistical error and neural network approximation error of value learning. sections.heading: A.1 Error Bounds for Parts I and II
sections.text: In this subsection, we derive upper bounds for Parts 𝐈 \mathbf{I} and 𝐈𝐈 \mathbf{II} in Lemma A.1 . These terms quantify the error caused by replacing the true soft optimal Bellman operator with its learned counterpart. As shown in Appendix B.4 , their bounds depend on the estimation errors of the conditional reward and transition distributions, together with the Monte-Carlo approximation errors in the construction of 𝒯 ^ α \widehat{{\cal T}}_{\alpha} . We begin by establishing a total variation bound for the conditional probability flow estimator. Since the true conditional distributions are supported on their prescribed domains, coordinatewise clipping leaves them unchanged. By the data-processing inequality for total variation, clipping the generated outputs therefore cannot increase their TV errors relative to these target distributions. Hence, it suffices to analyze the flow outputs before clipping. The total variation error can be decomposed as TV 2 ( p ^ t K ( ⋅ | S , A ) , p 1 ( ⋅ | S , A ) ) \displaystyle\mathrm{TV}^{2}\Big(\widehat{p}_{t_{K}}(\cdot|S,A),p_{1}(\cdot|S,A)\Big) ≲ TV 2 ( p ^ t K ( ⋅ | S , A ) , p 1 − τ ( ⋅ | S , A ) ) \displaystyle\lesssim\mathrm{TV}^{2}\Big(\widehat{p}_{t_{K}}(\cdot|S,A),p_{1-\tau}(\cdot|S,A)\Big) (3) + TV 2 ( p 1 − τ ( ⋅ | S , A ) , p 1 ( ⋅ | S , A ) ) . \displaystyle+\mathrm{TV}^{2}\Big(p_{1-\tau}(\cdot|S,A),p_{1}(\cdot|S,A)\Big). Here, p 1 − τ ( ⋅ | S , A ) p_{1-\tau}(\cdot|S,A) is the marginal density generated by the exact probability flow at time 1 − τ 1-\tau , while p ^ t K ( ⋅ | S , A ) \widehat{p}_{t_{K}}(\cdot|S,A) is the density generated by the learned flow under the EM scheme before clipping, with t K = 1 − τ t_{K}=1-\tau . The first term in ( 3 ) captures the combined effects of Gaussian initialization, score estimation, and numerical discretization. The second term is the terminal smoothing bias resulting from stopping the flow at time 1 − τ 1-\tau . We bound these two terms separately below.

sections.text: In this part, we bound the first term in ( 3 ). This term compares the EM discretized conditional flow induced by the learned score estimate with the exact conditional probability flow. For each fixed ( s , a ) (s,a) , the exact density p t ( ⋅ | s , a ) p_{t}(\cdot|s,a) solves the transport equation with velocity field u ∗ ​ ( ⋅ , t , s , a ) u^{*}(\cdot,t,s,a) , while the EM interpolated density p ^ t ( ⋅ | s , a ) \widehat{p}_{t}(\cdot|s,a) solves a transport equation with the frozen velocity field u ^ ​ ( Φ k , t − 1 ​ ( ⋅ ) , t k , s , a ) \widehat{u}(\Phi_{k,t}^{-1}(\cdot),t_{k},s,a) on each interval [ t k , t k + 1 ] [t_{k},t_{k+1}] . In addition to the initial density difference caused by Gaussian initialization, the transport equations introduce two error terms: the score-estimation error u ^ ​ ( x , t , s , a ) − u ∗ ​ ( x , t , s , a ) = 2 − t 2 ​ t ​ ( s ⁡ ( x , t , s , a ) − ∇ x ​ log ​ p t ​ ( x | s , a ) ) \widehat{u}(x,t,s,a)-u^{*}(x,t,s,a)=\frac{2-t}{2t}\big(s(x,t,s,a)-\nabla_{x}\log p_{t}(x|s,a)\big) , and the EM discretization error u ^ ​ ( Φ k , t − 1 ​ ( x ) , t k , s , a ) − u ^ ​ ( x , t , s , a ) \widehat{u}(\Phi_{k,t}^{-1}(x),t_{k},s,a)-\widehat{u}(x,t,s,a) . Following the L 1 L^{1} stability strategy for probability flow ODEs in ( Huang et al., 2025 ) , we control the density difference by the transport equation stability estimate. The score estimation part is bounded by the Gagliardo–Nirenberg interpolation inequality, while the discretization part is controlled by the regularity of the learned velocity field and the step size Δ \Delta . This yields the following conditional learned EM flow error bound. Lemma A.2 . Suppose Assumptions 4.1 , 4.2 , and 4.3 hold. Assume that L τ = 𝒪 ⁡ ( τ − 1 ) L_{\tau}={\cal O}(\tau^{-1}) and Δ = o ⁡ ( τ 2 ) \Delta=o(\tau^{2}) as τ \tau tends to zero. Then 𝔼 𝔻 x , 𝕋 , ℤ 𝔼 ( S , A ) TV 2 ( p ^ t K ( ⋅ | S , A ) , p 1 − τ ( ⋅ | S , A ) ) ≲ τ 2 1 − τ + ζ τ 4 + Δ 2 τ 8 log 2 τ . \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{D}_{x},\mathbb{T},\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{E}_{(S,A)}\mathrm{TV}^{2}\Big(\widehat{p}_{t_{K}}(\cdot|S,A),p_{1-\tau}(\cdot|S,A)\Big)\lesssim\frac{\tau^{2}}{1-\tau}+\frac{\zeta}{\tau^{4}}+\frac{\Delta^{2}}{\tau^{8}}\log^{2}\tau. Remark A.1 . The upper bound in Lemma A.2 separates Gaussian initialization error, score estimation error, and time discretization error. The initialization term is 𝒪 ⁡ ( τ 2 / ( 1 − τ ) ) \mathcal{O}\big(\tau^{2}/(1-\tau)\big) , as established directly in the proof. The term 𝒪 ⁡ ( ζ τ 4 ) \mathcal{O}\big(\frac{\zeta}{\tau^{4}}\big) accounts for the error from approximating the exact velocity field with the learned score function, while 𝒪 ⁡ ( Δ 2 τ 8 ​ log 2 ​ τ ) \mathcal{O}\big(\frac{\Delta^{2}}{\tau^{8}}\log^{2}\tau\big) captures the numerical error induced by the discrete EM scheme. Similar score and discretization error decompositions appear in probability flow ODE analyses ( Huang et al., 2025 ; Cai and Li, 2025 ; Gao and Zhu, 2025 , e.g.,) .

The bounds in Lemmas A.2 – A.3 together imply the following error bound for transition kernel estimation. Lemma A.4 . Suppose that the conditions of Lemmas A.2 – A.3 are satisfied. Then, 𝔼 𝔻 x , 𝕋 , ℤ 𝔼 ( S , A ) [ TV 2 ( 𝒫 ^ ( ⋅ | S , A ) , 𝒫 ( ⋅ | S , A ) ) ] ≲ ζ τ 4 + Δ 2 τ 8 log 2 τ + τ β ∧ 1 . \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{D}_{x},\mathbb{T},\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{E}_{(S,A)}\Big[\mathrm{TV}^{2}\Big(\widehat{\mathcal{P}}(\cdot|S,A),\mathcal{P}(\cdot|S,A)\Big)\Big]\lesssim\frac{\zeta}{\tau^{4}}+\frac{\Delta^{2}}{\tau^{8}}\log^{2}\tau+\tau^{\beta\wedge 1}. Under the conditions of Lemma A.4 with the same Hölder index β \beta , we have 𝔼 𝔻 r , 𝕋 , ℤ 𝔼 ( S , A ) [ TV 2 ( ℛ ^ ( ⋅ | S , A ) , ℛ ( ⋅ | S , A ) ) ] ≲ ζ τ 4 + Δ 2 τ 8 log 2 τ + τ β ∧ 1 . \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{D}_{r},\mathbb{T},\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{E}_{(S,A)}\Big[\mathrm{TV}^{2}\Big(\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(\cdot|S,A),\mathcal{R}(\cdot|S,A)\Big)\Big]\lesssim\frac{\zeta}{\tau^{4}}+\frac{\Delta^{2}}{\tau^{8}}\log^{2}\tau+\tau^{\beta\wedge 1}. sections.heading: A.2 Error Bound for Part III
sections.text: In this section, we analyze Part 𝐈𝐈𝐈 \mathbf{III} of the error decomposition in Lemma A.1 , which captures the error arising from value learning. It consists of the statistical error sup Q ∈ 𝒬 ( ℒ ⁡ ( 𝒯 ^ α , Q ) − 2 ​ ℒ ^ ​ ( 𝒯 ^ α , Q ) ) \sup\limits_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}}\big(\mathcal{L}(\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{\alpha};Q)-2\widehat{\mathcal{L}}(\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{\alpha};Q)\big) and the neural network approximation error inf Q ∈ 𝒬 ‖ Q − Q ∗ ‖ ∞ 2 . \inf\limits_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}}\|Q-Q^{*}\|_{\infty}^{2}. We derive bounds for these two terms separately and then combine them to obtain an upper bound on the Bellman residual risk error.

sections.heading: Bound statistical error sup Q ∈ 𝒬 ( ℒ ⁡ ( 𝒯 ^ α , Q ) − 2 ​ ℒ ^ ​ ( 𝒯 ^ α , Q ) ) \sup\limits_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}}\big(\mathcal{L}({\widehat{\mathcal{T}}}_{\alpha};Q)-2\widehat{\mathcal{L}}({\widehat{\mathcal{T}}}_{\alpha};Q)\big) .
sections.text: To establish the desired bound, we follow the proof strategy of Chen et al. (2023, Lemma 15) . Specifically, the infinite function class 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} is first approximated by a finite δ \delta -net, thereby reducing the uniform concentration problem to one over a finite collection of neural networks. The cardinality of this δ \delta -net is controlled using the covering number estimate in Feng et al. (2024, Lemma 20) . Substituting the prescribed network size, depth, width, and parameter bound into the resulting entropy estimate yields the following bound. Lemma A.5 . Assume that the class 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} of ReLU DNNs has size 𝒞 = 𝒪 ⁡ ( n d 2 ​ β + d ​ log ⁡ n ) \mathcal{C}=\mathcal{O}(n^{\frac{d}{2\beta+d}}\log n) , depth 𝒟 = 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) \mathcal{D}=\mathcal{O}(\log n) , width 𝒲 = 𝒪 ⁡ ( n d 2 ​ β + d ) \mathcal{W}=\mathcal{O}(n^{\frac{d}{2\beta+d}}) , and weight bound ℬ = 𝒪 ⁡ ( n d 2 ​ β + d ) \mathcal{B}=\mathcal{O}(n^{\frac{d}{2\beta+d}}) . Then 𝔼 𝕊 ​ sup Q ∈ 𝒬 ( ℒ ⁡ ( 𝒯 ^ α , Q ) − 2 ​ ℒ ^ ​ ( 𝒯 ^ α , Q ) ) ≲ Q max 2 ​ n − 2 ​ β 2 ​ β + d ​ log 3 ​ n . \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{S}}\sup_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}}\bigl(\mathcal{L}(\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{\alpha};Q)-2\widehat{\mathcal{L}}(\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{\alpha};Q)\bigr)\lesssim Q_{\max}^{2}n^{-\frac{2\beta}{2\beta+d}}\log^{3}n. Remark A.3 . To derive the statistical error bound in Lemma A.5 , we assume that the batch data are i.i.d., following the standard setting in the statistical analysis of deep reinforcement learning ( Jiang and Li, 2016 ; Fan et al., 2020 ; Uehara et al., 2022 ) . Our proof applies a concentration inequality to a finite δ \delta -net of the ReLU DNN class 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} and then extends the resulting bound to the full class through a covering-number argument. Under the network architecture and parameter choices specified in Lemma A.5 , this gives the rate 𝒪 ⁡ ( Q max 2 ​ n − 2 ​ β 2 ​ β + d ​ log 3 ​ n ) \mathcal{O}\bigl(Q_{\max}^{2}n^{-\frac{2\beta}{2\beta+d}}\log^{3}n\bigr) . The proposal and temperature parameters are fixed with respect to n n , and their dependence is absorbed into the implicit constant. Moreover, the i.i.d. assumption can be extended to dependent data by accounting for the sequential structure of MDP trajectories. A standard approach is to impose suitable mixing conditions and apply concentration results for dependent samples to establish the corresponding statistical error bound, as in Feng et al. (2023) ; Jiao et al. (2025) .

sections.heading: Bound approximation error inf Q ∈ 𝒬 ‖ Q − Q ∗ ‖ ∞ 2 \inf\limits_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}}\|Q-Q^{*}\|_{\infty}^{2} .
sections.text: For the soft optimal Bellman operator 𝒯 α ∗ {\cal T}_{\alpha}^{*} , approximate Bellman completeness typically requires the image 𝒯 α ∗ ​ 𝒬 {\cal T}_{\alpha}^{*}\mathcal{Q} to be uniformly well-approximated by 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} , as quantified by sup Q ∈ 𝒬 inf Q ~ ∈ 𝒬 ‖ Q ~ − 𝒯 α ∗ ​ Q ‖ ∞ \sup\limits_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}}\inf\limits_{\widetilde{Q}\in\mathcal{Q}}\|\widetilde{Q}-{\cal T}_{\alpha}^{*}Q\|_{\infty} . While standard in iterative value-based methods that repeatedly project Bellman updates onto 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} , this closure condition is not intrinsic to maximum entropy reinforcement learning. Indeed, recent works on entropy-regularized offline RL establish theoretical guarantees by replacing Bellman completeness with realizability conditions tailored to their specific estimators. For instance, Uehara et al. (2023) impose realizability on both Q ∗ Q^{*} and an auxiliary saddle-point function, whereas Zhan et al. (2022) analyze a regularized primal-dual formulation under realizability and single-policy concentrability. Our analysis takes a more direct route. Because the proposed framework explicitly estimates the reward distribution and transition kernel before minimizing the empirical soft Bellman residual, the error decomposition in Lemma A.1 reduces the approximation overhead to inf Q ∈ 𝒬 ‖ Q − Q ∗ ‖ ∞ 2 \inf\limits_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}}\|Q-Q^{*}\|_{\infty}^{2} , completely bypassing uniform closure conditions over 𝒯 α ∗ ​ 𝒬 {\cal T}_{\alpha}^{*}\mathcal{Q} . Consequently, it suffices to approximate the single target function Q ∗ Q^{*} , whose smoothness is guaranteed by the following result. Lemma A.6 . Suppose that the conditional reward and transition densities satisfy Assumption 4.4 . Then the optimal soft action-value function satisfies Q ∗ ∈ ℋ β Q^{*}\in{\cal H}^{\beta} . With the Hölder regularity from Lemma A.6 , we can directly invoke the deep ReLU network approximation theory of Jiao et al. (2025) to bound inf Q ∈ 𝒬 ‖ Q − Q ∗ ‖ ∞ 2 \inf\limits_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}}\|Q-Q^{*}\|_{\infty}^{2} (see Appendix C for the detailed derivation). Combining this approximation rate with the preceding statistical error bound yields Theorem 4.2 .

sections.heading: Appendix B Proof of Theorem 4.1
sections.text: We first address the two operator learning terms in Lemma A.1 . The argument controls the discrepancy between the learned and true conditional reward and transition laws, and then propagates these distributional errors, together with sampling errors, to the soft Bellman operator. This establishes the operator bound stated in Theorem 4.1 .

Email: zcmath@whu.edu.cn Abstract Offline maximum entropy reinforcement learning seeks to estimate the optimal soft action-value function Q ∗ Q^{*} from a fixed dataset without further interaction with the environment. Although Q ∗ Q^{*} is characterized by the soft optimal Bellman equation, the corresponding Bellman operator cannot be evaluated directly because both the reward distribution and the transition kernel are unknown. Consequently, estimating Q ∗ Q^{*} requires the joint treatment of environment modeling and value function learning. We propose a framework that addresses these tasks separately. Conditional diffusion models based on probability flow ODEs estimate the conditional reward distribution and transition kernel. The resulting distributional estimators define a data driven approximation of the soft optimal Bellman operator, whose empirical Bellman residual is minimized over a class of deep neural networks to estimate Q ∗ Q^{*} . This formulation separates high dimensional conditional distribution estimation from Bellman fixed point estimation while preserving the structure of the maximum entropy Bellman equation. We establish nonasymptotic guarantees for the proposed method. For operator learning, we derive total variation error bounds for the conditional flow estimators that account explicitly for score estimation, numerical discretization, and terminal smoothing. For soft value learning, we first use the soft Bellman equation to show that Q ∗ Q^{*} inherits Hölder regularity from the conditional reward and transition densities. For any Hölder index β \beta , the value learning stage achieves an excess Bellman residual risk bound of order 𝒪 ~ ​ ( n − 2 ​ β d + 2 ​ β ) , \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(n^{-\frac{2\beta}{d+2\beta}}\big), where d d is the total dimension of the state and action spaces. In contrast to many existing theoretical analyses of deep reinforcement learning, our results do not require Bellman completeness. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. KEY WORDS : Deep maximum entropy RL, Bellman residual minimization, Deep Q ∗ Q^{\ast} estimation, Conditional flow model. 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning (RL) studies sequential decision making in Markov decision processes, where an agent learns from observations, actions, and rewards to improve long-term performance ( Kaelbling et al., 1996 ; Sutton and Barto, 2018 ) . Classical methods represent value functions or policies explicitly, whereas deep reinforcement learning uses neural networks to handle large or continuous state and action spaces. This combination has enabled progress in visual control and game playing ( Mnih et al., 2015 ; Silver et al., 2016 ) , as well as applications to chip placement and plasma control ( Mirhoseini et al., 2021 ; Degrave et al., 2022 ) . These applications illustrate the flexibility of neural representations, while also making the statistical behavior of value estimation an important theoretical question. In value-based methods, the fitted target contains a continuation value estimated from data. Consequently, errors in Bellman-target construction interact with neural network approximation and empirical optimization. Actor-critic methods introduce a further interaction because policy updates depend on an estimated critic, while the critic is trained using data and targets associated with the policy ( Fujimoto et al., 2018 ; Haarnoja et al., 2018b ) . In the offline setting, the available dataset is fixed and additional environment interaction is unavailable. A useful analysis must explain how offline data are used to estimate the Bellman operator and how operator estimation error propagates to the learned value function. Maximum entropy RL augments the expected-return objective with policy entropy, encouraging stochastic policies while retaining a preference for actions with high expected return ( Ziebart et al., 2008 ; Haarnoja et al., 2018b ; Levine, 2018 ) . Entropy regularization replaces action maximization in the optimal Bellman equation with a log-partition operation. The resulting operator is associated with a Gibbs policy whose density depends on the soft action-value function ( Geist et al., 2019 ) . This structure connects value function estimation with policy optimization: the soft value summarizes an integral over actions, and the estimated action-value function determines the corresponding policy. Soft Q-learning develops this connection through energy-based policies and approximate inference ( Haarnoja et al., 2017 ; Levine, 2018 ) . Path Consistency Learning uses temporal consistency relations involving values and entropy-regularized action probabilities ( Nachum et al., 2017 ) , while Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) combines a stochastic actor, a soft critic, and replay data for continuous control ( Haarnoja et al., 2018b ; Haarnoja et al., 2018c ) . The relationship between policy gradients and soft Q-learning provides a complementary account of their shared optimality structure ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) . Soft policy-gradient methods and robust-control analyses further develop the algorithmic and theoretical consequences of entropy regularization ( Shi et al., 2019 ; Eysenbach and Levine, 2022 ) . For offline estimation, however, the soft Bellman operator still involves a conditional expectation over the unknown next-state distribution. Evaluating this expectation, together with the action integral, is the statistical and computational problem addressed by the present construction. Model-based RL provides a natural way to address this difficulty by explicitly learning the reward or transition dynamics from data and then using the learned model for planning, synthetic data generation, or Bellman evaluation ( Sutton and Barto, 2018 ; Janner et al., 2019 ; Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) . This paradigm is particularly attractive when real environment interaction is expensive or unavailable, since the learned dynamics can be queried repeatedly. Its central challenge is model bias: inaccuracies in the learned dynamics may accumulate over long imagined rollouts and can be amplified by subsequent policy optimization. Existing approaches such as MBPO, MOPO, and MOReL mitigate this effect through short model rollouts or conservative and uncertainty-aware objectives ( Janner et al., 2019 ; Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) . This perspective suggests learning the conditional next state law directly and using it locally to approximate the conditional expectation appearing in the soft Bellman operator. Recent advances in generative flow models have provided flexible tools for representing complex distributions in reinforcement learning. Existing flow based reinforcement learning methods mainly use flows on the decision side to model behavior policies, represent multimodal action distributions, or generate high value actions. For example, Flow Q Learning uses a flow matching policy to capture complex behavior distributions and introduces an auxiliary one step policy to avoid backpropagation through the full iterative sampling procedure ( Park et al., 2025 ) . Energy guided and value guided flow methods further combine generative flow sampling with value functions or energy signals to improve action generation and policy optimization ( Alles et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Feng et al., 2025 ) . These studies demonstrate the strong distributional modeling capability of flow models in reinforcement learning. However, this capability can also be used on the environment side. In particular, a conditional flow model can approximate the full transition law P ⁡ ( S ′ | s , a ) P(S^{\prime}|s,a) rather than only predicting the conditional mean of the next state. Repeated samples generated from the learned transition law can then be used to approximate the conditional expectation appearing in the soft Bellman operator. Motivated by these developments, we propose a framework for offline maximum entropy value learning that integrates conditional probability flow modeling with soft Bellman residual risk. Conditional probability flow ODEs estimate the conditional reward law and transition law from batch data. The learned reward and transition distributions are incorporated into the soft optimal Bellman operator. With the learned environment model held fixed, the optimal soft action value function Q ∗ Q^{*} is estimated by minimizing the empirical soft Bellman residual over a ReLU DNN class. Unlike existing flow based reinforcement learning methods that mainly use flow models to represent policies or generate actions, our flow models operate on the environment side and model both the reward and the next state conditional on ( s , a ) (s,a) . This construction separates environment law estimation from soft Bellman residual risk, enables repeated sampling from the learned reward and transition distributions, and avoids jointly optimizing the environment model and the value function within a single coupled objective. We derive a nonasymptotic bound on the squared Bellman-residual risk. The bound separates the error in the learned operator from the statistical and approximation terms associated with residual minimization. Under the stated conditions, the latter terms are of order O ~ ( n − 2 β / ( d + 2 β ) ) \widetilde{O}(n^{-2\beta/(d+2\beta)}) , where n n is the value learning sample size, d d is the state-action dimension, and β \beta is the Hölder smoothness of Q ∗ Q^{*} . Importantly, our analysis does not require the Bellman completeness assumption commonly adopted in theoretical studies of deep reinforcement learning ( Uehara et al., 2023 ; Zhan et al., 2022 ) . Empirically, we evaluate the proposed method in three experimental settings: a simulated MDP, classical control tasks, and HalfCheetah datasets from D4RL ( Fu et al., 2020 ) . We compare the proposed method with SAC ( Haarnoja et al., 2018a ) , CQL ( Kumar et al., 2020 ) , and MOPO ( Yu et al., 2020 ) . The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of using conditional probability flow models to estimate the reward and transition laws and support the separation of environment law estimation from soft value function learning. 1.1 Contributions The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows. • We develop a framework for offline maximum entropy RL that separates conditional environment modeling from soft value learning. Conditional probability flow ODEs learn the reward distribution and transition kernel, and samples generated from these models define a data-driven approximation of the soft optimal Bellman operator. We then estimate Q ∗ Q^{\ast} by minimizing the empirical soft Bellman residual over a class of ReLU DNNs. This formulation allows the environment modeling and value learning errors to be analyzed separately. Numerical results show that the proposed method achieves competitive performance across the considered offline control tasks. • We decompose the error of the proposed estimator into operator estimation and value learning terms. The operator error is controlled by total variation bounds for the learned reward and transition laws. We further establish that the Hölder regularity of the conditional densities with respect to the state-action variables is inherited by Q ∗ Q^{*} through the soft Bellman equation. This result yields rates for the value learning stage without a separate smoothness assumption on Q ∗ Q^{*} or a Bellman completeness condition. Combining these results, we obtain nonasymptotic bounds on the operator estimation error and the Bellman residual risk of the resulting action-value estimator. 1.2 Related Work Deep RL and Max Entropy RL. DRL combines sequential decision making with neural function approximation, allowing value functions and policies to be learned from high dimensional observations ( Sutton and Barto, 2018 ; Mnih et al., 2015 ) . Its main difficulty is that the learning target is endogenous: a value estimate is reused to construct later temporal difference targets, while a policy update changes the distribution from which future data are collected ( Sutton and Barto, 2018 ; Jiao et al., 2025 ) . DRL algorithms therefore differ largely in how they control errors, distribution shift, and the interaction between policy evaluation and policy improvement ( Sutton and Barto, 2018 ; Mnih et al., 2015 ; Jiao et al., 2025 ) . In discrete action spaces, DQN established a practical value-based template by combining a convolutional Q-network with experience replay and a slowly updated target network ( Mnih et al., 2015 ) . Replay improves data reuse and weakens short range temporal dependence, whereas the target network slows the change of the Bellman target ( Mnih et al., 2015 ) . Double DQN reduces maximization bias by separating action selection from action evaluation ( van Hasselt et al., 2016 ) ; the dueling architecture decomposes the output into state value and advantage streams ( Wang et al., 2016 ) ; and distributional RL models the return distribution rather than only its expectation ( Bellemare et al., 2017 ) . These refinements improve target construction or representation, but the learned Q-function is still defined through a recursive Bellman relation and remains sensitive to approximation error in weakly sampled regions ( Sutton and Barto, 2018 ; Fujimoto et al., 2018 ; Jiao et al., 2025 ) . Maximum entropy RL modifies this conventional objective by maximizing expected return together with the policy entropy. The resulting soft Bellman backup replaces action maximization by a log-sum-exp (or log partition) operation, and its optimal policy is the corresponding Gibbs distribution ( Ziebart et al., 2008 ; Levine, 2018 ; Geist et al., 2019 ) . This formulation preserves multiple competitive actions, which can improve exploration and robustness when the value landscape is multimodal. In deep continuous-control settings, soft Q-learning introduced energy-based stochastic policies ( Haarnoja et al., 2017 ) , while SAC made the maximum entropy objective practical through off policy replay, separate actor and critic networks, and an adaptive temperature variant ( Haarnoja et al., 2018b ; Haarnoja et al., 2018c ) . Path Consistency Learning offers a complementary view by enforcing multi-step soft consistency between values and entropy regularized policy probabilities ( Nachum et al., 2017 ) . These methods differ in parameterization and optimization, but all use entropy regularization to couple policy improvement with soft value estimation. Further studies have expanded both the algorithmic and theoretical foundations of learning with entropy regularization. The equivalence between policy gradient methods and soft Q-learning reveals that maximum entropy methods based on value functions and those based on policies share the same underlying optimization structure ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) . Deep Soft Policy Gradient provides an alternative implementation of the maximum entropy objective in continuous action spaces by combining actor and critic networks with off-policy learning ( Shi et al., 2019 ) . For offline learning, minimax soft-Q learning provides guarantees under realizability and partial coverage ( Uehara et al., 2023 ) ; separately, robust control results show that MaxEnt RL can solve classes of RL problems with reward and transition uncertainty ( Eysenbach and Levine, 2022 ) . Together, these studies connect entropy regularization to algorithm design and statistical guarantees, while leaving open the question of how transition model error affects soft Bellman value learning. Continuous control makes explicit maximization over actions impractical and motivates policy gradient and actor–critic methods ( Konda and Tsitsiklis, 1999 ; Silver et al., 2014 ) . In an actor–critic architecture, the actor represents the policy, while the critic estimates a value or advantage used to reduce gradient variance ( Konda and Tsitsiklis, 1999 ; Mnih et al., 2016 ) . This two line organization is flexible, but it creates coupled optimization: the critic is fitted using data from a changing actor, and the actor is updated using a critic that is only approximately accurate ( Konda and Tsitsiklis, 1999 ; Fujimoto et al., 2018 ) . Deterministic policy gradient methods differentiate the critic with respect to the action and backpropagate this derivative through the actor ( Silver et al., 2014 ) . DDPG combines this mechanism with replay and target networks to obtain an off policy algorithm for continuous actions ( Lillicrap et al., 2016 ) . Its deterministic actor is efficient, but exploration must be injected separately and the actor may exploit local overestimation in the critic ( Lillicrap et al., 2016 ; Fujimoto et al., 2018 ) . TD3 addresses this failure mode through clipped double-Q targets, delayed actor updates, and target policy smoothing ( Fujimoto et al., 2018 ) . These changes improve robustness without removing the fundamental dependence of policy improvement on an estimated critic ( Fujimoto et al., 2018 ) . Explicit environment modeling is central to our setting. Direct DRL methods construct Bellman targets from observed transitions without first estimating a separate transition kernel, whereas model-based methods estimate rewards or dynamics and use the learned model for planning, synthetic data generation, or Bellman evaluation ( Sutton and Barto, 2018 ; Janner et al., 2019 ; Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) . Explicit modeling can improve data reuse, but inaccurate models may be exploited by the policy and multi-step rollouts can accumulate error ( Janner et al., 2019 ; Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) . MBPO limits this effect with short rollouts initialized from real data ( Janner et al., 2019 ) ; MOPO and MOReL introduce pessimism or uncertainty control in offline model-based learning ( Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) . Our framework learns the conditional next state law, but uses it only for the one step expectation in the soft Bellman operator rather than for long imagined trajectories. This localized construction makes transition error visible at the operator level and separates it from the statistical and approximation errors of Bellman residual value estimation, in contrast to the repeated model rollout used in MBPO, MOPO, and MOReL ( Janner et al., 2019 ; Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) . Flow-based RL. Generative modeling has broadened the policy and trajectory distributions available to RL algorithms ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2025 ) . A conventional continuous control actor is often a deterministic map or a diagonal Gaussian distribution ( Lillicrap et al., 2016 ; Haarnoja et al., 2018b ) . Although computationally convenient, such a representation can be inadequate when a state admits several qualitatively different yet individually valid actions; a unimodal actor may average incompatible modes and place mass on actions that are poorly supported by the data ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2023 ; Celik et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2025 ) . Diffusion and flow matching models instead transport a simple reference distribution into a complex conditional distribution, making multimodal action sequences, policies, or trajectories directly representable ( Song et al., 2021 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ; Albergo et al., 2025 ) . This flexibility is particularly attractive in offline RL, goal conditioned control, imitation learning, and robotic manipulation, where datasets may contain several successful behavioral strategies ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2025 ) . For flow-based generative policies in particular, direct policy improvement through an iterative flow remains difficult because the terminal action depends on every integration step ( Park et al., 2025 ; Alles et al., 2025 ) . Flow Q-Learning (FQL) separates distribution modeling from Q-based improvement ( Park et al., 2025 ) . It first fits a flow matching policy to a potentially multimodal behavior distribution, then trains an auxiliary one-step policy with a Q-learning objective and links the two through a distillation style loss ( Park et al., 2025 ) . The construction avoids backpropagating the RL objective through the complete flow trajectory and removes iterative sampling at test time ( Park et al., 2025 ) . The flow supplies an expressive behavioral prior, whereas the one-step policy provides a tractable object for value improvement ( Park et al., 2025 ) . Importantly, the flow in FQL models the conditional action distribution and is therefore a policy generator, not an estimator of the environment transition law ( Park et al., 2025 ) . A second group of methods incorporates energy or value information directly into the probability path. FlowQ absorbs energy guidance into the learned velocity field rather than repeatedly applying an external guidance term during inference ( Alles et al., 2025 ) . Energy weighted flow matching reweights the flow objective so that the terminal distribution approximates an energy tilted reference distribution, with a learned Q-function providing the energy in offline RL ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . General analyses of flow guidance describe how conditional expectations, energy gradients, and approximations of intermediate guided marginals determine the corrected velocity field ( Feng et al., 2025 ) . Diffusion guidance can likewise be interpreted as a controllable policy improvement operator, where the guidance scale balances fidelity to a reference generator against movement toward critic preferred actions ( Frans et al., 2025 ) . Maximum entropy approaches such as DIME and MaxEntDP use expressive diffusion policies to retain multiple high value action modes rather than collapsing to a single deterministic decision ( Celik et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2025 ) . These methods primarily improve the representation of the policy π ⁡ ( a | s ) \pi(a|s) ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2025 ; Alles et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Celik et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2025 ) . They do not, by themselves, identify the environmental transition law P ⁡ ( s ′ | s , a ) P(s^{\prime}|s,a) , because the generators in these methods are trained as action or trajectory models rather than conditional next state models ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2025 ; Alles et al., 2025 ) . This distinction is essential for maximum entropy value learning because the soft Bellman target contains both an action side log partition operation and an expectation over the next state distribution ( Haarnoja et al., 2018b ; Geist et al., 2019 ) . An action flow can generate diverse actions, but without environment interaction or a separate dynamics model it cannot generate corresponding next states ( Park et al., 2025 ; Alles et al., 2025 ) ; conversely, a learned transition model can sample next states conditional on ( s , a ) (s,a) but does not automatically define an improved policy ( Janner et al., 2019 ; Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) . Policy flow methods therefore address multimodal action representation and value guidance, whereas our method addresses conditional transition estimation and the effect of transition error on the soft Bellman operator ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2025 ; Alles et al., 2025 ; Janner et al., 2019 ; Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) . In contrast, our method uses flows to learn the reward and transition distributions, which are then used to construct an empirical Bellman operator for value function learning. 2 Preliminaries 2.1 Markov Decision Process A discounted Markov decision process (MDP) is described by ( 𝒮 , 𝒜 , P , ℛ , γ ) ({\cal S},{\cal A},P,{\cal R},\gamma) .
